opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's wonderful work, and I'm glad people are doing it. But you have to look at what formal verification actually gives you. You can prove that a piece of code satisfies a specification, and that's very valuable for narrow, well-defined systems. The problem is that the guarantee is only as good as the specification, the verifier, and the world model you're verifying against.

First, the specification. What exactly do you want to prove? "The system will not harm humans"? Define harm. Define human. Define "will not" across every possible future situation, including ones we can't imagine because the system is smarter than us. We don't know how to write that down formally, and if we write down something slightly wrong, we have a mathematically guaranteed system doing the wrong thing perfectly.

Second, the verifier itself. A proof is checked by software, and that software can have bugs. You can verify the verifier, but then you need to verify that, and you get an infinite regress. At some point you just trust something. With mathematical proofs we see the same thing: the longer and more complex the proof, the less confident we are that it's correct. Proofs about a system with trillions of parameters, interacting with the real world, are a very different beast from proving a sorting algorithm correct.

Third, the world model. These approaches typically say: we'll have a model of the world and prove the AI's actions are safe with respect to it. But the world isn't a formal system. Physics has gaps, humans are unpredictable, and a superintelligent agent may find aspects of reality that aren't in your model at all. Your guarantee only covers the model you wrote.

And then there's the part I keep coming back to: this isn't a static system. It learns, it self-modifies, it interacts with other agents, it's under attack from malevolent actors. Even if you verified version one, you need guarantees that hold through every update, forever. A permanent solution means getting it right on every iteration, with no chance to learn from a failure, because one failure with a superintelligent system could be the last one.

So at best you get a probabilistic, local guarantee: this component, under these assumptions, with this specification, is probably correct. That's useful for making today's systems better. But as a permanent answer to controlling something smarter than us, I just don't see it. You can't fully verify, predict, or explain such a system, and from that, in my view, it follows that you can't indefinitely control it either.

r001.rationale: It says formal verification offers only probabilistic, local guarantees and cannot be a permanent answer to controlling a superintelligent system.

r002.rationale: It does not claim that improving safety guarantees toward perfection requires exponentially increasing resources.

r003.rationale: It says one failure could be catastrophic, but does not connect residual risk to an enormous number of decisions over the system’s lifetime.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I actually think it's a very nice paper, and the people behind it are serious, and I want to be clear I'm not dismissing the work. But I think there is a fundamental confusion about what verification can give you, and it's important to separate the levels.

Formal verification works beautifully for a specific piece of software with a specific specification in a fixed environment. You can prove that this sorting algorithm sorts, that this compiler preserves semantics. Even there, we have decades of experience and the proofs are only as good as the specification, and the specification is where the bugs usually are. Now scale that up. What is the specification for "safe"? For "aligned with human values"? Nobody can write it down. We don't agree on what the values are, they change over time, they differ between cultures, between individuals. So you would be proving a very precise theorem about a very imprecise thing.

Then there is the issue of the world model. These approaches typically say, we'll have a model of the environment, and we'll verify the AI's actions are safe with respect to that model. But the world is not the model. The system interacts with physics, with people, with other AI systems, and any gap between the model and reality is where things go wrong. And a sufficiently capable system is exactly the kind of agent that finds those gaps. So you've proven safety in the map, not in the territory.

And then there is the question of who verifies the verifier. The proof checker, the hardware it runs on, the humans interpreting the result, the training process that produced the model you are checking, the deployment pipeline. Every layer adds a possibility of error. We already see in cybersecurity that formally verified systems get compromised because the attack comes from a direction nobody included in the threat model.

But I think the deepest issue is that safety is not a property you establish once. It is something you have to maintain forever, against a system that keeps learning, keeps changing, keeps getting more capable, and operates in an environment that also keeps changing. You can verify a snapshot. You cannot verify the future. If the system is self-modifying, or if we are continuously training new versions, then every verification is a verification of yesterday's system. And with superintelligence, you would need the guarantee to hold not for a year, not for ten years, but indefinitely, with zero failures, because one failure could be unrecoverable. No engineering discipline has ever achieved that. We don't have bug-free software of any meaningful size. We don't have perfectly secure systems. We have systems that are good enough, with acceptable failure rates. Here the acceptable failure rate is zero and the time horizon is infinite.

So my view is that these methods can reduce risk, they can buy us something, maybe they help with narrow systems, with tool AI, with constrained domains. That's valuable. But as a permanent solution to the control problem for general superintelligence, I think it's closer to a hope than a plan. And I would rather we were honest about that than tell ourselves we have a proof when what we actually have is a proof about a different, simpler problem.

r001.rationale: It says the acceptable failure rate for superintelligent AI is zero and that verification cannot guarantee safety indefinitely.

r002.rationale: It does not say that improving safety guarantees requires exponentially increasing resources.

r003.rationale: It says one failure could be unrecoverable and discusses an infinite time horizon, but does not connect residual risk to an enormous number of decisions over the system’s lifetime.

astra-6.text:
Because a proof is always conditional. You prove that a particular system satisfies a particular specification under a set of assumptions. You haven’t proved that the specification captures everything we mean by safety, or that those assumptions will continue to hold in the real world.

Take the specification problem. We don’t have a complete formal definition of what humanity wants. We disagree, our preferences change, and there are situations we haven’t imagined. If you formalize the wrong objective, you can prove that the system will reliably do something you don’t actually want.

Then there’s the gap between the model and reality. Your proof might be mathematically correct, but the system operates through hardware, sensors, other software, and people. A guarantee about a model extends to the world only insofar as the model’s assumptions are valid.

So I think formal verification is useful. You can establish specific properties of bounded systems. But that’s different from permanently guaranteeing the safety of a general intelligence that learns, changes, and acts in an open environment. The difficult question is always: what exactly did you prove, and under which assumptions? Calling something guaranteed safe doesn’t remove those limits.

r001.rationale: It says a proof is conditional and that formal verification cannot permanently guarantee the safety of a general intelligence in an open environment.

r002.rationale: It does not say that improving safety guarantees requires exponentially increasing resources.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that residual risk becomes consequential because the system makes an enormous number of decisions over its lifetime.

sol-6.1.text:
Formal verification can tell you that a system satisfies a particular specification under particular assumptions. But that’s a conditional guarantee. How do you know the specification captures everything we mean by safety? How do you know the assumptions will continue to hold when the system interacts with the real world?

You could prove that an AI never takes some forbidden action and still discover that it achieves a harmful outcome through something you forgot to forbid. The proof can be correct while the specification is inadequate.

And if the system learns, modifies itself, or operates in a changing environment, you have to establish that your guarantees continue to apply. You can sometimes prove properties across those changes, but again, only within a model. The world is not obligated to stay inside your model.

So I think this research is useful. We should verify the properties we can verify. But going from that to a permanent guarantee that a superintelligent system will never harm humanity is a much stronger claim. You haven’t eliminated the safety problem; you’ve moved part of it into the specification and the assumptions.

r001.rationale: It says formal verification cannot provide a permanent guarantee that a superintelligent system will never harm humanity, communicating that it cannot guarantee perfect AI safety.

r002.rationale: It does not say that improving guarantees toward perfection requires exponentially increasing resources.

r003.rationale: It does not connect residual risk to an enormous number of decisions over the system’s lifetime.
